The examples fix which bit each task looks at and which input pairs get which button. They do not fix whether button 1 in the new task means "neither bit is 1" or the opposite. Below, "bit" means bit position 1–4, counted left to right.

**Y components (which bit each one reads)**
- **Y3 is bit 4.** In X1-Y3-Z3, every example gives 0 when the two bit-4 values match and 3 when they differ. In X1-Y3-Z1, matching gives 3 and differing gives 2.
- **Y4 is bit 3.** In X1-Y4-Z3, matching bit-3 values give 0 and differing ones give 3. In X3-Y4-Z4, the button is 1 exactly when both bit-3 values are 1, and 3 otherwise.
- **Y2 is bit 2.** In X4-Y2-Z1, the button is 3 exactly when both bit-2 values are 0, and 2 otherwise. In X5-Y2-Z3, matching gives 3 and differing gives 0.

**Assignments that fit all six known tasks**

X1 must be either "both are the same" or "exactly one is 1". That choice fixes the meanings of Z1, Z3, X4 and X5. X3 can still be "both are 1" or "not both are 1", which sets Z4.

| | X1 | X4 | X5 | X3 | Z4 (true / false) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | same | neither | exactly one | both | 1 / 3 |
| B | same | neither | exactly one | not both | 3 / 1 |
| C | exactly one | at least one | same | both | 1 / 3 |
| D | exactly one | at least one | same | not both | 3 / 1 |

All four keep different versions of each component distinct.

**What this means for X4-Y3-Z4 (bit 4)**
- Under A and D, the button is 1 when neither bit 4 is 1, and 3 otherwise.
- Under B and C, the button is 3 when neither bit 4 is 1, and 1 otherwise.

I looked for a pattern across components, such as button 3 always meaning true or always meaning false. No assignment is consistent on that, so none of the four is more plausible than the others. The answer is undetermined, and each option is about a 50/50 guess. I chose A/D, so neither→1.

Only inputs 7, 9 and 12 have bit 4 equal to 0 in both stimuli. They get button 1 and every other input gets button 3.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: 0, 1, 2, or 3. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> 2` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is 2.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
